“You have this conflict between individual incentives and science as a whole,” says [James Evans](https://sociology.uchicago.edu/directory/james-evans), a sociologist at the University of Chicago who led the study.

And as more researchers pile onto the same scientific bandwagons, some experts worry about a feedback loop of conformity and declining originality. “This is very problematic,” says [Luís Nunes Amaral](https://www.mccormick.northwestern.edu/research-faculty/directory/profiles/amaral-luis-a-nunes.html), a physicist who studies complex systems at [Northwestern University](https://spectrum.ieee.org/tag/northwestern-university). “We are digging the same hole deeper and deeper.”

Evans and his colleagues [published the findings](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-09922-y) 14 January in the journal *Nature*.

For Evans, the tension between efficiency and exploration is familiar terrain. He has spent more than a decade using massive publication and citation datasets to [quantify how ideas spread](https://www.science.org/doi/full/10.1126/science.aao0185), stall, and sometimes converge.
